title: 2026 SEND Explorer Virtual User Group Meeting
body_markdown:
ShareShareShare


### View transcript


*This is not a verbatim transcript.*


Melissa Cunningham — Welcome and opening


Hey. Good morning, and good afternoon, everyone. My name is Melissa Cunningham. I’m the product owner of the SEND Explorer application, and I wanted to welcome you to our fourth annual user group meeting. Whether this is your first or fourth meeting, I am thrilled to see each of you here today.


This is really one of our favorite days of the year. We get to see so many customers in one place, show you what’s new, and just as important to get your feedback.


As the team and I were putting this event together, there was a lot of time to reflect over the past year. And one word kept coming to mind, and that is change, change and evolution.


And this is really the theme that you will see running throughout our presentation today.


As we look at our industry and even our home life, AI has really taken over. It’s been a tool that people are using, whether it’s in the pharmaceutical industry, biotech, or even in the regulatory space, it’s impacting the way we are working. And you’ll see that in SEND Explorer today, where it stands, and where we’re taking it in the future.


There’s also a lot of novelty and new things happening in nonclinical space. There’s real momentum around new approach methodologies or NAMS, utilizing your interim study analysis, looking to see if you can use virtual control animals to replace animals in your studies and also in the predictive toxicology space. And I’m sure that you are starting to see or seeing these changes within your own organizations.


My team has changed too. Peggy and Joyce have retired. And I personally want to thank them for everything that they’ve done to get NextGen to where we are today, and for all of their assistance with each of you throughout the years.


We’ve been very fortunate though to have Samantha Marden joining us, who’s going to introduce herself very shortly.


And the product itself is evolving too. NextGen is going to be available at the end of this month. It’s a major rewrite. It’s been a humongous undertaking, and I’m very proud of both the product and development teams who have put everything into this latest release to make it happen.


We’ve been a little bit quieter than usual because of this feat, but I’m really looking forward to the upcoming year when we can start working closely together with each of you to implement the new changes.


I do hope that today inspires you as you see the direction that the product is taking and how it can change your day-to-day activities as you interpret your studies.


With me today, I have the pleasure of co speaking with Kevin Snyder, who’s the Director of Nonclinical Innovation and Emerging Technologies Jamie Gilliam, who is a Senior Product Manager on the SEND Explorer team, and Samantha Marden, who is a Product Manager on the SEND Explorer team as well.


I do have a few housekeeping topics to discuss though before we get to our content. Our aim is to wrap up on time and stick to our schedule.


We ask that everybody mute their lines. We do hope that you will ask questions. On the upper right hand side of GoToWebinar, there is a question feature.


In the off chance that you experience technical issues, please use the chat feature, also on the upper right hand side, and the marketing team will try to assist you. We’ll be recording our session today, and we will make that link available to you about a week from now via email. And we do love feedback. Whether it’s questions about the content that you’re seeing today or anything else, please feel free to reach out, and we hope that you’ll fill out the survey at the conclusion of today’s presentation.


A little bit about today’s agenda. Samantha is going to walk us through SEND 4.0, what’s happening and what the impact will look like. Jamie is going to give a great walkthrough of the NextGen workflow and some of the new features that will be available to you.


Kevin will give a talk called, is it real? Is it relevant? Is it safe? Contextualizing your toxicology data with the SEND Explorer data lake. I’ll follow it up with upgrade details and a little bit more about our road map for version 13.1 and version 14. The team is going to gather to take questions, and then I’ll do a very brief wrap up.


But for those of you on the call that are a little bit newer to the Certara family, I wanted to speak a little bit about our mission, and that is to solve complex challenges in drug discovery and development through scientific expertise, advanced biosimulation, and innovative technologies.


We’re very proud to have 2,600 companies that we support and 23 global agencies that have adopted our technology.


We have over twenty years of industry leadership and innovation experience, and fifteen hundred employees call Certara home, four hundred and thirty of which have their PhD. And we’re spread throughout 33 countries across the world. It’s a really great place to work.


But more importantly, I am very proud that we are able to partner with each of you to bring lifesaving medicines to our patients in need. More than 90% of all novel drugs approved by the US FDA since 2014 were supported either through our services or technology.


And then finally, I wanted to just share some of our applications that we have and services. So at the center of this is SEND Explorer, or I like to think it is.


But really, Certara offers a fully integrated suite of solutions that span the entire drug development life cycle from discovery through launch and post market.


And this slide really illustrates how our platforms and consulting services really work together to accelerate development and improve decision making.


On the left-hand side of the screen, you see Certara IQ. And this is an AI powered QSP platform, and it helps to predict biological responses.


We also have Chemaxon, which is a chem informatics suite of tools with a design hub, and it fully integrates into D360. This is an application that can aggregate all of your research data in one place.


But as we start moving into the preclinical space that we’re all much more familiar with, we start seeing deeper modeling and simulation with our Simcyp platform. And for those of you on the call that are DMPK scientists, we have Phoenix, which is our PKPD platform for analysis and modeling, and that’s moved to the cloud this year, which has been very exciting for that team.


We also have Pinnacle 21, and this can help validate your data before it goes into SEND Explorer or before a submission.


We also have GlobalSubmit to help with submissions and CoAuthor. I did want to call them out because this can really help facilitate your report writing and even creation of CTD tables. So it can be a huge time saver for those tasks that take a lot of time.


We have two applications that aren’t shown on this slide as well that are quite helpful in the preclinical space. We have something called Tox Studio, where you can predict toxicological outcomes using in silico technologies, and this can help benefit streamlining your workflows, and also reducing the number of animals used in testing.


And we also have DIDB, which is the Drug Interaction Database. It’s the industry’s largest scientifically curated database to assess drug interactions and safety.


If you’re interested in any of the different applications or services that we offer, you can get in contact with your sales rep. Certara.com also has a lot more information, or I personally am very happy to put you in contact with the right colleague.


With that, I am going to turn it over to Samantha. She’s going to run through our first polling question of the day and then discuss SEND 4.0.


Thank you.


Samantha Marden — SEND 4.0 overview


Hello, everybody. The first polling question for the day is where is your organization and its preparation for SEND 4.0?


Whether you started planning, you haven’t started planning, you have no idea what Send is, and this is all foreign, give you a couple of seconds to answer the question.


Okay, it looks like most people are still assessing the impact on your current SEND data sets. Some haven’t started planning and some are actively updating their processes. Good.


So again, hi, everybody. My name is Samantha Marden. I am a manager of product management for SEND Explorer. I’ve been with Certara for about five months, and my background is in veterinary, science and research along with years of experience in SEND datasets and submissions. And I will be discussing the next major release of the SENDIG 4.0.


For those of you who do not know, SEND stands for the standard for exchange of nonclinical data. SEND specifies a way to collect and present nonclinical data in a consistent format and is one of the required standards for data submission to the FDA. Version 4.0 is the largest revision of the guide since SEND was introduced.


It changes the domains you submit, many of the variables inside them, and the underlying approach to how nonstandard data is represented. My goal today is to give you a clearer picture of differences from version 3.1.1 and what that means for your studies and your data pipelines. One note to keep in mind is this overview is based on the current 4.0 revision history, public review comments are still being worked through, and some items are still marked as in progress. So because of this, some details may shift before final publication.


Here’s the scale of the 4.0 changes in five numbers. Nine new domains are being added, which significantly broadens the nonclinical data SEND can carry. Two domains are being deprecated.


Roughly 40 new variable concepts are being introduced, many of which are added to several domains at once, creating numerous new domain level variable entries. For those of you, again, that don’t know, a variable is a specific column or data field within a domain that represents a measured, counted, or descriptive attribute of a study subject.


On the other hand, 49 existing variables are being removed, and around 200 variable labels have been standardized. This will allow the variables to be more consistent across the standard.


And beyond the numbers, there are several structural changes that we will also cover.


One of the most important changes in 4.0 is the expansion of the scope the SEND model will now be able to cover.


Until now, SEND has been strongest for the core general toxicology endpoints, body weights, clinical observations, clinical pathology, and macroscopic and microscopic pathology. Data from many specialty assessments either didn’t fit the standard or had to be force fit through custom domains. Version 4.0 changes that. Along with nine new domains, it includes an appendix that defines the scope of the standard.


That appendix sets out which study types and endpoints the CDISC SEND team considers confidently modeled. So what’s new? SEND will expand into immunology with two new domains. Cell phenotype findings covers immunophenotyping data.


Immunogenicity specimen assessment covers anti-drug antibody, or ADA, data and similar assessments. These were formerly in the LB domain, and together they now have clear guidance on where data should be represented.


Genetic toxicology in vivo brings the in vivo genotoxicity results into SEND.


The new nervous system findings domain gives a home for neurobehavioral data, including the functional observational battery data. FOB data has historically been among the hardest to standardize because there are a mix of observations, counts, and scored assessments, and every lab records them a little differently.


With NV, alongside the new scoring scales domain for documenting scoring systems, FOB results can be submitted in a consistent, reviewable format.


The new ophthalmic examinations and skin test results domains are dedicated to targeted eye and dermal assessments. These were formally put into the CL domain.


Pharmacokinetics input documents the concentration data and transformations behind your PK parameters, which makes the path from PC to PP more easily traceable. And the nonstandard variables domain replaces the use of supplemental qualifier domains completely.


Finally, two domains have been removed: body weight gain and tumor findings, along with a tumor. xpt mapping appendix.


These changes allow for more of your study data to be submitted in a standard form, which means more of it can be reviewed with standard tools.


So what about changes to existing domains?


Exposure changes significantly and can now represent doses that were not administered. Clinical observations now explicitly covers assumptions of qualitative food and water consumption. For example, changes in appetite are presented in the CL domain, while qualitative food and water consumption has been moved to the FW domain. Any results that are not part of routine clinical observations and are from specifically targeted tests like I just mentioned must now be reported in their respective domains and not in CL.


Demographics moves to numeric age ranges and adds an example for subjects who were never dosed. Organ measurements now supports in life measurements. And across the safety pharmacology domains, you’ll see new variables, continuous vital signs data and arrhythmia count guidance.


Microscopic findings is substantially expanded with new sections for carcinogenicity studies, sexual maturity, reproductive cycle phase evaluation, and targeted staining, each with its own assumptions and examples. Masses are now linked across domains using Mass ID with new follow-up record conventions.


For PK, transformations move to the new PI domain, and there are new examples for biodistribution in gene therapy studies and tissue concentrations.


The trial design domains now have more support for multiple test articles, and there are new examples for Latin square designs with and without washout and for split-scope designs.


On the data model, the guide has been rewritten in ways that will change how your teams read and apply it. Wherever the guide supports a conformance rule, should is now must. So practices your teams treated as recommendations may now very well be requirements.


The domain specification tables have also been redesigned to align with SDTM version 3.0, and each domain now opens with an overview table so you know exactly what a domain is for before you look at a single variable. The guide has also been restructured for easier navigation and the file extension is no longer restricted to XPT format. It is important to note that the FDA’s requirements may still differ from CDISC in terms of what format is allowable for submission.


In section four of the new guide, the general assumptions has gained a set of new topics that answer some longstanding questions. This section’s main purpose is to provide guidance when it comes to dealing with complex data scenarios.


These include how to use the sequence number, how to represent multiple values in one variable, a much more detailed description of how to create a custom domain amongst many others. More information on section four can be found directly in the implementation guide.


Four appendices will provide new reference material, but two may directly stand out to you and your needs. Appendix A combines the trial summary and trial set codes and adds a structured description for treatment vehicles.


So what does this mean for CROs and sponsors? Appendix A allows for one standard approach to trial summaries and trial sets and uses such an approach across multiple datasets. Vehicle composition is also then described the same way everywhere. This means study setup is faster, there are fewer sponsor specific exceptions, it is easier to compare control groups and treatment arms across studies, and there’s less rework when validation findings come back.


Appendix C defines the scope of version 4.0, meaning which study types and endpoints the CDISC send team considers confidently modeled. This helps you plan and can give clearer references for scoping at much earlier study stages, like protocols.


CROs and sponsors will know upfront which endpoints and studies are in scope of SEND, out of scope, or which may need use of custom domains. This can help with contracts and data transfer agreements, as well as reduce surprises at time of submission.


SEND 4.0 isn’t a change to one dataset or one domain. Every change together reaches almost every part of how SEND data will be produced, checked, and delivered.


Mapping specifications, programs, data transfers, and authoring software all need to support 4.0’s new domains, variables, and code lists. The same updates are required for the viewers, reports, and scripts.


Updated send conformance rules and core designations will change your validation reports, so plan time to resolve new findings.


QC checklists, comparison programs, and training need to account for the new content, and drop checks for retired domains and variables.


Define-XML will have several updates, so get familiar with the new Define-XML appendix. And finally, update your SOPs and templates. For some time, you will likely support both versions side by side, where 3.1.1 is for ongoing studies and 4.0 is for new ones.


Every SEND process will touch 4.0. So our recommended next step, start with a gap assessment of your current SEND outputs against 4.0. Talk with your teams about their readiness timelines. Update your mapping specifications and templates. Pilot a 4.0 on a representative study before you need it for submission and keep an eye on regulatory acceptance dates so that your transition is timed to when agencies will require or accept the newest version. We’re happy to support you with any of these steps.


And how will those of us at Certara be ready? We are very involved in the CDISC SEND team, including any and all revisions to the IG. We have been closely monitoring all the content changes to make sure that we stay informed. In terms of SEND Explorer, some of the changes that come with 4.0 may change some of the visualizations you are used to, especially in terms of baseline data. Our development team and product team are working together to ensure that SEND Explorer can be prepared to handle the new domains, variables, and processes.


So when is SEND 4.0 expected? As of right now, SEND 4.0 is estimated to be published at the end of Q1 for 2027.


And while 4.0 develops and finalizes, we plan to keep you all updated with any SEND 4.0 news and how it will affect SEND Explorer and your datasets.


As a reminder, please note that any information I’ve shared today is still based on that current SEND IG 4.0 revision history, and some details are still subject to change before final publication. For more information on SEND 4.0, feel free to head over to the CDISC public wiki page where you can read more on the upcoming changes and expectations. The link included on this slide will be available once this presentation is shared.


And now I will hand you guys over to Jamie.


Thank you, Samantha.


Jamie — NextGen workflow and demonstration


Good morning, good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining. I’m Jamie Gillam, senior manager of product management for SEND Explorer here at Certara. If you were in attendance at last year’s UGM, we gave you a preview of the new features and the automated endpoints of interest functionality. We’re very proud of the progress that we’ve made in the past year. So during this session, I will talk about the enhancements, especially with the endpoints of interest workflow. Then I’m going to finish with a live demo so that you’re able to see the new navigation in action.


So let’s get started then. The concept of an endpoint of interest is present in SEND Explorer version 12. This is a special feature that allows users to flag specific endpoints while you’re reviewing the data. The biggest benefit in version 12 is the ability to filter by the endpoints of interest in different visualizations and summaries.


And this really focuses your attention on the important aspects of the data.


SEND Explorer NextGen introduces some very exciting enhancements, and I’m going to highlight those both in the slides and during the demonstration.


I’m going to walk through what a data review process might look like if you’re using SEND Explorer and the endpoints of interest functionality.


So currently, though, version 12 allows for manual flagging of numeric endpoints and tissues of interest. SEND Explorer NextGen retains all of that existing functionality, but it also allows for manual flagging of clinical observation findings from either the ClinObs time course or the subject view. For gross and histopathology data, not only can tissues be flagged, but now specific findings for a tissue can also be flagged.


All the user approved endpoints of interest for a single study will still appear on the study overview page and also on the multi study endpoints of interest grid view. So that’s still available and where you’ll see the global list of all of the endpoints of interest that have been flagged for all of the studies within your SEND Explorer application.


In addition to those, SEND Explorer NextGen has a new Endpoints of Interest details page, which we’ll see in more detail in a minute here in the demo.


But a major part of the new functionality that we’re the most excited about is the ability to auto flag the endpoints of interest. So the user can execute permissive statistical analysis that will automatically flag endpoints of interest.


This analysis is done for numeric clinical pathology and organ weight data, and then also for your gross and histopathology data. Any endpoint that meets the established criteria will be marked as pending for a further scientific review. The automated analysis methods do assume that the study design is a repeat dose toxicity study and that the sponsor group codes are ordered by ascending dose with the control group first. The auto flagging is not yet recommended for other study designs or if there are multiple treatments used in the study.


While these automated methods of identifying pending endpoints of interest don’t cover all study designs and data types yet, users can still take advantage of the workflow by manually flagging those endpoints.


So the auto flagging for LB and OM numeric endpoints applies an overall ANOVA followed by a two tailed Dunnet’s test.


And the comparison is between the control group and the high dose group. This is done separately for males and females, and it’s only done at the last time point for which data are present prior to the start of a recovery phase.


Additionally, numeric endpoints are auto flagged if the group mean values are strictly increasing or strictly decreasing across all dose groups, again assessed separately for males and females.


For the MA and MI pathology domains, the auto flagging algorithm is going to calculate a metric separately for the control group and the high dose group. This is done for each combination of tissue and finding for subjects with a terminal disposition.


If the calculated metric for the high dose group is at least 1.5 times the calculated metric for the control group for a given sex, then the associated finding is flagged as a finding of interest for that occurrence of a finding and if the high dose group has at least one occurrence, that finding will be flagged for review.


And it is important to note that the calculated metric used for auto flagging does not consider findings in any dose group other than the first and the last or the control and the high dose group. And it doesn’t look at findings associated with subjects with any disposition other than terminal sacrifice.


Okay, so there’s just a few other important details I wanted to share before moving on to the demo. This slide shows the endpoints of interest workflow.


It’s important to note that the auto flagging process is not automatically generated during the study upload, but it is executed on demand by the user. And this is intentional for several reasons, one of which is there may be legacy studies for which users do not want to auto generate those endpoints of interest. But once a user clicks generate to initiate the analysis, the endpoints that meet the criteria are marked with the status of pending. As part of your review process, you can opt to approve, ignore, or simply leave endpoints as pending for further review.


There’s also the ability to add clarifying free text comments to any of the endpoints.


And during the review, the endpoints can also be manually added. What I haven’t mentioned yet is the AI summarization piece, and this is the last step in the workflow, and it will generate a summary based on a prompt and the approved endpoints of interests. So the endpoints of interests workflow can be done as soon as you start receiving data for an ongoing study, all the way through to report generation and beyond, maybe when you want to start doing cross study analysis.


Okay, so then I am going to move on to the demo portion here.


This is the NextGen SEND Explorer dashboard that you see.


So, SEND Explorer NextGen brings a refreshed interface, which includes a new navigation panel for moving between studies and visualizations.


In this demo, I will highlight the navigation changes, but primarily I will focus on the endpoints of interest process. You will see how the pending endpoints are flagged automatically, and then how the approved endpoints, along with the prompt, result in an AI summary. As we go, I really encourage you to think about where this process fits into your existing data review workflow and where it will save you time.


Upon logging in, the dashboard is still the landing page. Users can access the studies using the hyperlink in the Study ID column.


Each of the columns can be filtered and sorted. You can do more advanced filtering using other fields, and you can filter for studies that share a common interest. But new on the dashboard is the Select column here on the left-hand side.


And this column is going to allow me to check the box for a study or a group of studies, and then certain visualizations will allow filtering for just those studies that are selected on the dashboard. This is a time saver if you are reviewing multiple studies for maybe a specific compound or a program. I’ll go ahead and select a couple here just so we can take a look at it in a minute.


You may have noticed that the options in my top ribbon have changed, and the Multi Study and Visualization tabs are no longer present. By using the three bars here on the left-hand corner, the new navigation menu appears. We have links to the home page and the dashboard pages at the top. Then we have tabs for single study and multi study. Right now, the focus is on the single study tab, and you can see the study pull down menu. At the top will be the last five studies that were recently viewed in the system.


Any studies that I had selected on the dashboard are present in the Dashboard section, and then there is a complete list of the studies that are available in this particular database. The filter field allows for a search of the available studies, and as I type, it is going to limit my options, and I’m going to limit to the INDS06. And when a study is selected, my navigation menu is populated with links to the Overview page here, the new Endpoints of Interest details page, followed by all of the different visualizations, the group summary and listings, and then at the bottom here, the metadata domains. Now these are all the views that are applicable for the selected study.


So, if I just take a look quickly at the Multi-Study tab, this displays all of the Multi Study enabled visualizations. So, we’ll first take a look then at the overview page for INDS06.


And the Overview page presents the metadata about the study, and these metadata are sourced from the SEND datasets. This page has undergone a redesign, including reordering of several sections, although first we still see the key study information followed by the Notes, Images, and Links section.


But instead of what was the test subject information in version 12, we now see a redesigned study table. And this table reflects Send Explorer’s interpretation of the study design, and it’s intended to correspond with the experimental design table that appears in study protocols. So this table identifies the planned groups, the treatment, dose levels, route of administration, as well as the planned disposition events.


The next section then is the Disposition Summary table.


This table presents the actual disposition information, and by default, it is displaying the mortality counts that you see here, and those are present for each disposition event for the entire study duration. The grouping is by sex. We can see males and females, and then within that, the group and dose level. If I wanted to view the breakdown by study day or study week, I can use the time option, and I’ll first select by day. And now we can see on the left hand side the study day for each of the disposition events. And if I wanted to see them by study week, it will then roll that up into the study weeks.


To display the counts for just unscheduled deaths, I can use the toggle at the top for unscheduled.


And then in the totals drop down here, I’m going to select both. And now I have two total rows at the bottom of the table, one with the count, and then the other is the percent of the animals that had an unscheduled death in each group for each study week.


Okay. So let me use the reset button here to return it to the default, and I want to switch to the Survival option.


Using the Survival option, the death statuses no longer appear, and my count has now switched to cumulative. If I select a time of by week and choose percent instead of count, now the table shows the percent of animals that are alive for each of my groups during each of the study weeks.


So this is a finalized study, so we would expect zero percent survival in the last week. However, this is a useful view for users who are looking at ongoing studies.


Overall, this table really does provide many options for customization, and both of these tables can be copied to your clipboard and then pasted into another document for use.


The remainder of the overview page is the same as version 12 with the additional study metadata information. If we take a look at the right side here, we see the grid for the endpoints of interest, and this is the next topic that we’ll take a look at.


And as I mentioned, the endpoints of interest functionality has been vastly improved in the NextGen version of SEND Explorer, and it’s been enhanced with an AI component. So from my navigation panel, I’m going to select a new study.


I’ll go ahead and take a look at this study, and I’m going to go to the endpoints of interest page.


And you can see here that the auto generation has not yet been done for this particular study because the auto generation process is initiated by the user. This is done by clicking the Generate option. So the auto flagging process will be applied to clinical pathology and organ weight data. Keep in mind numeric data for other endpoints can be manually flagged. Once the analysis has finished, by default we’re seeing the results for the numeric endpoints, and each of them has a pending status.


The grid is showing me the domain and the test codes, and then I have separate columns for males and females here.


If we take a look at these columns, this column will show the result of the Dunnett’s test. And then hovering over a particular cell, I can see even more details about that particular test.


It’s a little touchy on the screen here. There we go.


The next column then is our trend column. And when the group mean values are strictly increasing or decreasing, there will be arrows in this column to show the trend. Now these trends may sometimes be more informative because the analysis is being done across all of the dose groups.


The high dose group means are shown as fold of control, so you can see that separately here for males and females. And then the last two columns are Edit and Status. As you’re scrolling through the grid initially to get a sense of what endpoints stand interesting, you can use the links in the Edit column to approve, ignore, or edit a finding.


The information in the Status column lets me know if an endpoint has been approved and by whom, or if it’s still pending or ignored.


As I’m analyzing these endpoints of interest, I have the ability to drill down to the actual data.


So these test codes that you see here are hyperlinked to the Summary by Timepoint view. And we’ll go ahead and look at one here. I’m going to open it in a different browser window.


And this is going to be the Summary by Timepoint for the LB domain or the clinical pathology data. And drilling down to the summary data allows me to then look across multiple time points for all of my groups. I can review calculated change from baseline measures if those are present. I can look for outliers, and then I could also drill down to individual subject values if necessary. So in this example, the MCHC endpoint was flagged as a pending endpoint of interest based on the analysis on Day 90, which is the end of the dosing period for this study. And now I can look at the data in the recovery phase to determine if there is still an effect.


I will come back to the summary views in a minute to talk a little bit more about some of the navigation changes. However, before we go back to the endpoints of interest details page, I wanted to point out how manually flagging endpoints can happen in this particular view. You can see there is a flag here, and this is going to allow me to approve the test as an endpoint of interest or edit one that’s already been approved.


Back on my Endpoints of Interest details page, at the top of the page, there is a Clinical Observations tab.


Now, the clinical observations endpoints of interest will not be auto generated. Findings must be flagged by the user, and they can be flagged in the ClinObs time course or subject view. But once a finding has been selected, it will then display on this page. At the top of the grid here, you see a link, and this option is going to allow me to view the ClinObs time course visualization. So we’ll go ahead and open that up.


And this initial view is all of the findings for this particular study with separate plots for each of the findings by sex. Now, the Findings dropdown here is where I can flag my findings of interest, and that’s done by clicking this flag icon in line with a specific finding. So we’ll go ahead and click a couple here just to add that there. Okay. And then at the top of this box is a filter option.


So I can choose this flag to then filter for just those findings of interest, and now the plot has been limited to findings of interest. And it’s a very useful way of focusing in on key aspects of the study.


So I’m going to use the navigation to go back to my endpoints of interest for this particular study, and if I go to the Clinical Observations tab, you can then see those two findings that I had added in the time course visualization.


Next at the top, we have the pathology findings tab. Now the system automatically generated an initial set of findings of interest.


The algorithm determined if there was an increase in either the incidence and or severity in the high dose group that is significantly different from the control group. Those that met the criteria are listed here as pending.


The grid presents the different tissues and then the findings within each tissue separate for males and females. I can use the edit column again to approve, ignore, or edit each row, and then the status will be present here.


And any of those that are approved are going to be shown on the Study Overview page, and they will be part of the filtering in several visualizations.


The links at the top of this particular tab will open the severity heat map, either for macroscopic findings or the microscopic findings, and that’s going to allow us to see more details about the specimens and findings as a whole. So clicking the link here for the view of the severity heat map for histopathology, we’ll go ahead and take a look at this.


I now have a view that’s limited to the findings and tissues that have been either approved or are still pending as endpoints of interest. So in my left-hand panel under the data selection options are the tissues of interest, and you can see the approved and the pending tissues are selected. I simply need to check the not identified, and this option then shows all of the histo data for this study. And then I can scroll through the screen here and take a look at the additional findings and tissues.


I could then flag the findings or tissues of interest manually. If I wanted to flag the tissue of heart, I can do that by clicking on the flag icon that you see here.
